REASONS FOR DECISION

The Case

[
1
]

This case is about school arrangements for Abby
age eight and Ben age seven.  Their parents, who have often been able to cooperate
in raising their children, have had to resort to a trial in order to resolve
the issue.

The Decision

[
2
]

On June 19, 2008, I delivered an endorsement
declaring that Abby and Ben would attend Woodland Public
School in Thornhill, Ontario, beginning September 2008.

[
3
]

At the outset of the trial, the schooling
issue was not the only issue to be decided because any order changing the children’s
current school would of necessity, involve issues of access, extra-curricular
activities, and possibly, the choice of health-care providers.  In addition,
the applicant, Lisa, was seeking sole custody.

[
4
]

Given the concessions made during the trial
by both parties and the evidence presented, I was confident that once a
decision on the schooling issue was rendered, the parents themselves, with the
assistance of their counsel, would be able to settle all the other outstanding
issues.  I proposed to the parties that they attempt to resolve those issues
and suggested that they take 30 days to attempt to negotiate.

[
5
]

Given counsel’s schedules through June and July
2008, counsel requested an extension to July 30th.  I approved this extension.

[
6
]

On July 31, 2008, I was advised that the
parties had, indeed, resolved all other outstanding matters by way of minutes
of settlement dated July 30, 2008.  I have reviewed the minutes of settlement,
which appear to have addressed all of the outstanding issues except for costs
of the trial.  There will, therefore, be an order issued in terms of the
minutes of settlement filed.

[
7
]

I now intend to deliver my reasons with
respect to the order that I made on June 19, 2008.  Once these reasons are
released, the parties will be given an opportunity to address the issue of
costs.

The Issues

[
8
]

As the case deals with an incident of
custody, any decision made must focus on the best interests of Abby and Ben.

[
9
]

In focusing on the best interests of Abby
and Ben, I have been asked by both parents to consider whether the children’s
Jewish identity can best be preserved through attendance at Uxbridge Public School
[1]
— which they have been
attending — or at Woodland Public School
[2]

which is close to their mother’s house.  Throughout the trial and during the
submissions made, both parents accepted as a given, that raising their children
in the Jewish faith was in their children’s best interests.  Notwithstanding
this, there still existed the question of whether a change in schools would
affect their stability and, therefore, their best interests.

[
10
]

There were also other factual and legal issues
that were raised by the parties; I shall deal with them in due course in these
reasons.

The Factual Background

[
11
]

In setting out the background facts of this
case, my intention is to have this background accepted as findings of fact.  If
there is a fact that is in dispute, or a contrary finding of a fact made, I
shall point that out and deal with it at the appropriate time.  I must say,
however, in a general way that in most important areas, there was agreement on
the facts between the parties.

[
12
]

Lisa Libbus was born on July 19, 1967 and is
41 years old.  She was raised in a Jewish home in Montreal, in a predominately Jewish neighbourhood.  She attended both a
public and Hebrew day school.  The public school had many Jewish students.  She
is bilingual (English and French).

[
13
]

Lisa attended the University of Western Ontario in London, Ontario from 1986
to 1989 and graduated with a degree in biochemistry.  While attending Western
she was involved in Jewish life on campus through campus organizations.
Consistent with her Jewish upbringing, she celebrated major Jewish holidays
with her family in Montreal.

[
14
]

Lisa moved to Toronto in 1989 to live and pursue further education.  She is now a
practicing physiotherapist.

[
15
]

Lisa met Bill through a mutual friend in or
about April 1990.  At that time, Lisa was living in a rental apartment in the
Beaches area of Toronto.  By July
1991, Lisa and Bill each felt confident enough about their relationship to move
in together into Lisa’s apartment.

[
16
]

Bill is 45 years old having been born in 1963.
Bill was raised in Breslau, Ontario, a small town not far from Kitchener,
Ontario.  He attended school in his community and in Kitchener.  He moved to Toronto for his university education where
he earned a Bachelor of Arts degree from York
University.  Bill was raised in a Roman Catholic home.

[
17
]

Bill is now an acting captain with the
Toronto Fire Department; he has been a firefighter since 1990.

[
18
]

Bill and Lisa lived in various places in the
Toronto area while Lisa
completed her formal education.  Towards the end of 1996, they purchased a new
house in Uxbridge, Ontario at 45
Bolton Drive.  An important consideration was cost.
They had explored staying in the Toronto area but found the cost of housing very expensive.  As it took
about a year to build the house, Bill and Lisa did not move to Uxbridge until December
1997.

[
19
]

During the courtship phase of their
relationship, Lisa and Bill took part in family celebrations, which included
Jewish holidays such as Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, and Passover.  They attended
celebratory and traditional meals with family members and friends.

[
20
]

When visiting Bill’s mother, Lisa and Bill
would take part in Christmas events.  Lisa attended midnight mass at Christmas
out of respect for Bill’s mother.  She describes Bill’s mother, Gladys, as very
kind-hearted and very close to Bill.

[
21
]

Bill proposed to Lisa in July 1997 while
they were on a trip to Paris;
they married on July 5, 1998.

[
22
]

The marriage took place at the University of Toronto Faculty Club.  The
ceremony was Jewish in nature.  The parties were married under a traditional “
chupah
”
by a rabbi.
[3]

Bill broke a small glass of wine with his foot, which is also a tradition in
the Jewish faith.  The parties signed a traditional Jewish marriage contract
called a “
ketubah
”.
[4]

[
23
]

Prior to beginning a family, Bill and Lisa discussed
the religious upbringing of any children they would have.  Bill was aware of
the fact that according to the Jewish faith, the children borne to a Jewish
mother would be considered Jewish.  He readily agreed that any children would
be raised as Jewish children in the Jewish faith.

[
24
]

Lisa became pregnant shortly after the
marriage.  She conducted an internet search to find a synagogue that would
accept couples and families that had intermarried.  She was able to find a
reform synagogue that suited her family’s purpose in Newmarket called “Or Hadash”.

[
25
]

Bill attended prenatal classes during Lisa’s
pregnancy.  He also participated in a
baby

naming
ceremony for
Abby at Or Hadash Synagogue.
[5]

In the Jewish tradition,
a baby naming
confers a Hebrew name upon a
female child.

[
26
]

After Abby’s birth, Lisa took maternity
leave for about eight months.  Bill was fully involved in Abby’s care as well.
He changed diapers and often played with Abby.  Lisa nursed Abby; Bill would
frequently bottle feed Abby after she had been weaned.

[
27
]

Lisa took an eight-week session on a number
of different topics dealing with baby care.  She involved Abby in music lessons
at the local library.  Bill attended some sessions.

[
28
]

When Ben was born, Lisa once again took
eight months off to be home with him.  When Ben was ten days old, he had a
circumcision ceremony in accordance with Jewish tradition.  The ceremony was performed
by an orthodox Jewish doctor who was ordained to perform such services.  Bill
willingly participated.

[
29
]

In terms of childcare, Bill was as fully
involved with Ben as he had been with Abby.  At that time, he worked seven, ten-hour
days and seven, fourteen-hour nights.  He was able to spend a considerable
period of time at home assisting with the children.  While Lisa may have been
the principal caregiver during the two maternity leave periods, it is clear
from the evidence that Bill participated as much as he could and as much as his
work schedule would allow.  He clearly co-parented along with Lisa.

[
30
]

Bill’s mother, Gladys, was often available
to assist with childcare.  During Lisa’s maternity leaves, Gladys was not
called upon as much as she would be later.

[
31
]

Bill and Lisa attended Or Hadash on an
infrequent basis when the children were young.  As there was no Jewish
influence in the Uxbridge community, the children, when they were very young,
were exposed to Judaism at Or Hadash, through some Jewish symbols in the house,
and through family celebrations at major religious holidays.  These holidays
were frequently celebrated together with Lisa’s family members.  Bill was
always included and willingly attended.

[
32
]

Lisa’s evidence was that when the children
were quite young, she began to feel an increased sense of isolation and
alienation in the community.  She and Bill could not help but notice that during
the Christmas season their house was one of the very few, if not the only house
in the neighbourhood, that did not display visible indications of Christmas.

[
33
]

After her maternity leave for Ben concluded,
Lisa, who had been employed, decided to open her own physiotherapist practice
in Uxbridge.  She had worked as a physiotherapist in Newmarket.  In October 2001 as the opportunities in Uxbridge seemed good,
Lisa opened her own practice.  Given the fact that Uxbridge was a commuter
community, Lisa worked from 12:00 p.m. to 8:00 p.m., Monday to Thursday and
Friday mornings.

[
34
]

When Lisa was not available to care for the
children, either Bill or Gladys or both were available.  It was Lisa’s evidence
that Gladys would assist “several” times a week.

[
35
]

After about six months (by April 2002), Lisa
was able to hire another physiotherapist.  This enabled her to change her hours
two mornings a week, from 9:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. or 3:00 p.m. on Monday and
Wednesday.  On Tuesdays and Thursdays, she continued to work from 12:00 p.m. to
8:00 p.m.

[
36
]

About one year later, Lisa was able to hire
a third physiotherapist who worked Tuesday and Thursday mornings.

[
37
]

In September 2007, Lisa stopped working on
Tuesday and Thursdays so that she could spend more time with the children.

[
38
]

Lisa’s business progressed to the point
where she was able to hire an administrative assistant (November 2007).  The assistant’s
hours are Monday to Friday 8:30 a.m. to 11:30 a.m.

[
39
]

Bill’s employment with the Toronto Fire
Department has been quite steady.  He started in the Beaches, and remained
there for a number of years before being transferred to the upper Beaches.  In
the summer of 2007, he was promoted to acting captain and is now stationed in Scarborough.  His previous shift of
fourteen days (seven days and seven nights) out of every twenty-eight days
changed in January 2007 to seven twenty-four hour shifts every twenty-eight
days.  His work schedule has always enabled Bill to spend a considerable amount
of time with the children.

[
40
]

Lisa’s anxiety about the lack of anything
Jewish in the Uxbridge community was tempered by the fact that the children
were progressing well with childcare assistance from Gladys.  In addition, Lisa
enjoyed her home and, in the main, the Uxbridge community.  While she felt she
did not fit in, her children and work kept her sufficiently satisfied.

[
41
]

With respect to her feelings of alienation,
she, admittedly, did not share these with Bill.  Mostly, this occurred because
Lisa is a person who has difficulty expressing emotions to others.  She also
described Bill as a person who deals with problems by deferring them to another
time.  Their individual personalities appeared to inhibit problematic
discussions.

[
42
]

While Lisa testified about a couple of
incidents she viewed as anti-Semitic, there was very little of this.  She tried
to deal with her concerns by attempting to fit in and by not letting too many
people know she was Jewish.

[
43
]

A fear she did express to Bill was concern
about their children being exposed to anti-Semitism.  Bill told her that they
would deal with the issue, if and when, it occurred.

[
44
]

Abby started junior kindergarten at UPS in September
2003.  Even though Bolton Drive
was beyond the UPS catchment area,
[6]

it was chosen because it offered French immersion.  This was important to both
parents.

[
45
]

Ben started UPS in September 2005, which was
after the parties separated.

[
46
]

There were no Jewish teachers in the school
nor were there any other Jewish classmates in either child’s class.

[
47
]

Eventually, Bill and Lisa joined the Or Hadash
congregation in Newmarket.

[
48
]

Abby was registered for Hebrew school
sometime in the summer of 2004.  Newmarket is within 30 minutes of Uxbridge.  Hebrew school used to be every
Saturday from 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 noon, but is now held every Sunday from 9:30
a.m. to 12:30 p.m.

[
49
]

When Ben reached the appropriate age for enrolment
in Hebrew school, he too, was enrolled.  This was also after the separation.

[
50
]

Exposure to Jewish faith and culture for the
children continued through Or Hadash and its Hebrew school, its Friday night
dinners once a month, attendance at major religious observances on Rosh
Hashanah and Yom Kippur.  The children were also exposed to some religious
symbols in the home and celebrated Jewish holidays with Lisa’s family members.

[
51
]

The children would see other Jewish children
at Hebrew school but none in their community.

[
52
]

As time went on, both children were enrolled
in various extra-curricular activities in Uxbridge and other towns close by.
Both were progressing very well at UPS and at Or Hadash.

[
53
]

In or about 2003, Bill and Lisa discussed
moving from Bolton Drive.  Lisa
testified that she was feeling more and more isolated living on Bolton Drive.  These feelings led her to
become unhappy.  She testified that she hated the sense of alienation she was
feeling.  While she and Bill began discussing a move, Lisa did not share the
feelings she was having with Bill.  The main reason she expressed for a move
was that of needing more space.

[
54
]

In addition, both parties wanted to have
Gladys live with them as she was very close to her grandchildren and provided
excellent care.  Gladys had moved from Breslau to a rental apartment in Uxbridge
in 2000.

[
55
]

While the subject discussed was one of more
space, Lisa was becoming anxious about the children’s possible isolation from
the rest of the town and wanted to insulate them against any possible
anti-Semitic or bullying incidents that might occur in the future.

[
56
]

The parties purchased 12690 Lakeridge Road in July 2004.  The
sale closed on November 10, 2004.  The property was bought in joint tenancy.
At the time of the closing Abby was five and Ben was three.

[
57
]

Lakeridge is a rural property, situated on
ten acres of land.  It is near Sunderland in Brock Township.  In terms
of driving time, it is about fifteen minutes from the centre of Uxbridge.

[
58
]

The
h
ouse
itself contains three bedrooms with a separate building connected to the main
house by a breezeway for Gladys.

[
59
]

The house is located in the school catchment
area of Cannington.  However, prior to the move, it was determined that Abby
would be able to continue at UPS, at least for the remainder of the school
year.

[
60
]

The evidence of both parties makes it clear
that the children enjoy the Lakeridge house and surrounding woods.

The Separation

[
61
]

Lisa finally started to mention her
unhappiness to Bill but not until about one month after moving into Lakeridge.
She testified that she felt “no connection” and no sense of community.  She
said that she hated what she had become.  She felt very isolated.  While Lisa
did not expand much about relationship issues, she also testified that, as far
as she was concerned, the marriage was far from perfect.

[
62
]

When she raised some of the feelings she was
experiencing with Bill, he indicated that he wanted to try to work things out.
As a result, the couple attended counselling for about six weeks.

[
63
]

By mid-February 2005, Lisa decided that she
could not continue in the marriage.  This decision was very hurtful to Bill.
He felt as though he had been “hit by a freight train”.

[
64
]

In April 2005, Lisa physically moved from
Lakeridge to a town house in Uxbridge.  She had leased the premises on Prospect St. towards the end of February
2005 but it was not ready for occupancy until April 1
st
.

[
65
]

Lisa felt fortunate to obtain this rental as
it was close to UPS and to her office.  It had the added advantage of being in
the UPS catchment area.

[
66
]

While Lisa said she did not really want to
be in Uxbridge, she felt that the separation would be difficult enough on the
children and, therefore did not want to move further away.  In addition, Bill
and Lisa had not sorted out their property division so that, from a financial
point of view, buying a house closer to Toronto was out of the question.

[
67
]

Both Bill and Lisa gave evidence about how
difficult the separation discussion was with the children, especially, Abby.

The Separation Agreements

[
68
]

The first separation agreement was signed on
March 18, 2005.  Neither party retained a lawyer.  Lisa testified that she was
so consumed with guilt over the separation that she purchased a precedent
agreement from a store and just followed the template.  She just wanted to “get
it done”.

[
69
]

Lisa prepared the initial draft and Bill
made some changes that were incorporated in the final agreement.  There was
little discussion about the substance of the agreement.

[
70
]

Bill was insistent that they each have equal
time with the children; the agreement set out a joint custody regime with equal
sharing.  A paragraph restricting mobility and a review clause were added.

[
71
]

The second separation agreement was
concluded about two years later.  It is dated March 20, 2007.  This agreement
settled all outstanding property matters between the parties.  It also
confirmed the provisions of the earlier agreement.

[
72
]

At this time, Lisa received $107,500.00 for
her interest in the matrimonial home.  Title to Lakeridge was conveyed to Bill.

Other Significant Events

[
73
]

Other important events occurred that would
have an impact on the Libbus family.  They are as follows:

(a)

Lisa met Gary Finklestein through a Jewish
on-line dating service in October 2006.  This relationship blossomed, so much
so that Gary has moved in with
Lisa and they now plan to marry;

(b)

Lisa purchased a house in the north-eastern part
of Thornhill in May 2007 and moved into it in September 28, 2007;

(c)

Bill, after the separation, developed a close
relationship with Catherine Jacobson who, at one point, had been Abby’s kindergarten
teacher.  In July 2007, Catherine and her two children Sierra age 15, and Evan
age 12, moved into the Lakeridge house.

Events Leading Up To Contested Court
Case

[
74
]

On April 12, 2007, Lisa issued an
application for divorce.  As the application claimed only a divorce, some time
went by before there was any legal activity in the case.

[
75
]

On June 3, 2007, Lisa, by letter, advised
Bill that she had purchased a house in Thornhill and proposed that the
“custodial arrangement as per our separation agreement” be revisited.  She also
proposed that the children attend the local French immersion school in
Thornhill.  Mediation was raised as a possible process to assist the couple.

[
76
]

Bill’s reaction indicated that resolution of
the issue might prove difficult and, therefore, Lisa wrote to him on June 20
th

proposing the names of three mediators.

[
77
]

On June 22, 2007, Lisa received a letter
from Bill’s former lawyer indicating that she was in breach or was about to
breach the provisions of the parties’ separation agreement.  The letter
requested that Lisa sign a consent, which basically confirmed the provisions of
the custody provisions of the separation agreement and stated that neither
party would change the children’s school from UPS without the written consent
of the other.  The letter accused Lisa of deliberately misleading Bill and the
court, by means of the divorce application.  It stated that her “unilateral
action” was inappropriate and not in the best interests of the children.  It
also threatened court action.  The letter also put forth the names of two other
mediators in the Durham region
for Lisa’s consideration.

[
78
]

At that point, Lisa informed Bill that she
would be retaining counsel.

[
79
]

On July 18, 2007, Lisa delivered an amended application,
which set out the claim that she wanted the children’s school changed.  Bill
answered the claim.  By way of reply dated September 6, 2007, Lisa requested
sole custody of the children.  Unfortunately, a litigation battle had begun
that would culminate in a long and costly trial.

Discussion of the Issues

[
80
]

Since the parties have now resolved all
outstanding issues, including the fact that they will continue to share joint
custody of the children, the only issue to be addressed in these reasons for
decision is the one of schooling.

[
81
]

While many factual issues were raised by each
parent at trial, two of the more important issues relate to the children’s
Jewish identity and to the importance of a stable and known environment as
represented by the status quo.

[
82
]

All of the factual issues, in my view,
played out at trial against a background of two parents and an extended family
of child-focused, loving, caring, and concerned individuals.  If more parents
raised children as have Lisa and Bill, and the other important people involved
in this case, we would be a truly fortunate society.  The issue to be decided
was a difficult one, which tested the skills of each parent, quite severely at
times.  In my opinion, any conduct on either of their parts that might be found
wanting was conduct brought about by the adversarial nature of litigation, and
had very little, if anything to do with their parenting ability, which has been
exemplary.  Lisa and Bill are both excellent parents.

Lisa’s Position

[
83
]

Lisa states that she and Bill agreed to
bring Abby and Ben up as Jews.  She submits that if they continue at UPS, their
Jewish identity will suffer.  This would be contrary to their best interests.

Bill’s Position

[
84
]

Bill also agrees that he and Lisa agreed to
raise their children as Jews.  He says that he has done and will continue to do
whatever is necessary in order to fulfill this agreement.  He agrees with Lisa
that raising the children in the Jewish faith is in their best interests.  It
is his view that this can be accomplished by allowing the children to remain at
UPS.  He points out that the children have always gone to UPS and, therefore,
preserving that stability together with the exposure to Judaism from both
parents will enable them to grow within the Jewish faith and develop their
religious and ethnic identity without disrupting their stability.

The
Divorce Act

[
85
]

The starting point for the legal examination
of the issues raised is found in
section 16
of the
Divorce Act
which
states as follows:

[7]

16.  ORDER FOR CUSTODY

(1) A court of competent
jurisdiction may, on application by either or both spouses or by any other
person, make an order respecting the custody of or the access to, or the
custody of and access to, any or all children of the marriage.

INTERIM ORDER FOR CUSTODY

(2) Where an application is made
under subsection (1), the court may, on application by either or both spouses
or by any other person, make an interim order respecting the custody of or the
access to, or the custody of and access to, any or all children of the marriage
pending determination of the application under subsection (1).

APPLICATION BY OTHER PERSON

(3) A person, other than a spouse,
may not make an application under subsection (1) or (2) without leave of the
court.

JOINT CUSTODY OR ACCESS

(4) The court may make an order
under this section granting custody of, or access to, any or all children of
the marriage to any one or more persons.

ACCESS

(5) Unless the court orders
otherwise, a spouse who is granted access to a child of the marriage has the
right to make inquiries, and to be given information, as to the health,
education and welfare of the child.

TERMS AND CONDITIONS

(6) The court may make an order
under this section for a definite or indefinite period or until the happening
of a specified event and may impose such other terms, conditions or restrictions
in connection therewith as it thinks fit and just.

ORDER RESPECTING CHANGE OF
RESIDENCE

(7) Without limiting the
generality of subsection (6), the court may include in an order under this
section a term requiring any person who has custody of a child of the marriage
and who intends to change the place of residence of that child to notify, at
least thirty days before the change or within such other period before the
change as the court may specify, any person who is granted access to that child
of the change, the time at which the change will be made and the new place of
residence of the child.

FACTORS

(8) In making an order under this
section, the court shall take into consideration only the best interests of the
child of the marriage as determined by reference to the condition, means, needs
and other circumstances of the child.

PAST CONDUCT

(9) In making an order under this
section, the court shall not take into consideration the past conduct of any
person unless the conduct is relevant to the ability of that person to act as a
parent of a child.

MAXIMUM CONTACT

(10) In making an order under this
section, the court shall give effect to the principle that a child of the
marriage should have as much contact with each spouse as is consistent with the
best interests of the child and, for that purpose, shall take into
consideration the willingness of the person for whom custody is sought to
facilitate such contact.

[
86
]

While provincial legislation is not
applicable in this case, it is useful to have regard to the various factors set
out in the
Children’s Law Reform Act
,
subsection 24(2)
, which
particularizes the concept of best interests.
[8]

These factors are:

24(2)  BEST INTERESTS OF
CHILD  — The court shall consider all the child’s needs and
circumstances, including,

(a) the
love, affection and emotional ties between the child and,

(i) each person entitled to or claiming custody of or access to the
child,

(ii) other members of the child’s family who reside with the child,
and

(iii) persons involved in the child’s care and upbringing;

(b) the
child’s views and preferences, if they can reasonably be ascertained;

(c) the
length of time the child has lived in a stable home environment;

(d) the ability and willingness of each person applying for custody
of the child to provide the child with guidance and education, the necessaries
of life and any special needs of the child;

(e) any
plans proposed for the child’s care and upbringing;

(f) the permanence and stability of the family unit with which it is
proposed that the child will live;

(g) the ability of each person applying for custody of or access to
the child to act as a parent; and

(h) the relationship by blood or through an adoption order between
the child and each person who is a party to the application

[
87
]

Section 16
of the
Divorce Act
makes
it very clear that a court, in making any kind of custodial decision involving
children, must consider only the best interests of the children as determined
by reference to the conditions, means, needs, and other circumstances of the
child.  It should be noted that the legislative standard requires the court to
focus on best interests – not on what is good or better but on what is best for
them.  While the
Divorce Act
is vague, case law and provincial statutes
for years now have focused our courts and counsel on the factors to be raised
in examining the concept of best interests.

[
88
]

In writing these reasons, I have, therefore,
considered the evidence by focusing on the factors set out in items (a) through
(g) in
subsection 24(2)
of the
Children’s Law Reform Act
.  No one factor
has greater weight than the other, nor is one factor particularly determinative
of the particular issue before me.  In other words, the question or issue of
guidance and education is no more important a factor than the children’s stable
home environment.  The important consideration, in my view, is ensuring that
the court has carefully considered and weighed the factors so that a particular
factor is not ignored in reaching a decision.

[
89
]

As stated previously, both Lisa and Bill are

[

[

Dr. Mock points out that Judaism is not just a religion but also a
way of life, and a value system.  It has ethnic and cultural elements.  It has,
unfortunately, become “racialized” as a result of Nazi policy during the 1930’s
and 1940’s.  Adopting a Jewish identity is not restricted to religion only.
Many people who are not particularly religious identify themselves as Jews on a
cultural level.

[
155
]

Dr. Mock’s report sets out certain general principles in the
development of ethnic, racial, and religious identity.  It is these principles
that are found in various psychological studies on child development.

[
156
]

Ethnic awareness and identification begins in children at about the
age of three.  This first phase is labelled “awareness”.  Children at this
early age notice differences in others but without value judgement.  The second
phase is called “identification”.  This phase comes about when the child
recognizes the group to which he or she belongs.  The third phase, the
“preference” phase, comes about through awareness of the larger community or
the world outside and of the way various groups are treated.

[
157
]

The identification phase is instilled in children through such
things as parochial school and family practices.  While children may adopt
certain negative or positive feelings during this time, it is more likely that
they just accept things as they happen.

[
158
]

The last phase involves an understanding that some groups are valued
more than others.  It often involves a desire to become part of the preferred
group.  While this can be counteracted to some extent by what happens in the
home, the reinforcement or support that comes from the wider environment plays
a more important role.  Children, during this phase, do not like to be centred
out.  When a child is the only child who needs to be away for a religious
holiday, that child is likely to feel different and not in a positive way.  A
child’s peer group plays a crucial role during this time.  Families that are
trying to instil an identity have to work even harder with their child to
ensure that the child is receiving positive reinforcement so that the child
does not engage in self-hatred.  This is almost impossible to do unless the
child has a peer group that helps him or her feel that he or she is not second-class.
If the child is the only child whose parent comes to class to celebrate and
talk about the child’s holidays, the child often feels singled out.

A child is likely to feel proud about his or her identity if that
identity is reflected in the community and in the school curriculum.  If such
identity is not so reflected, the child is likely to feel marginalized,
notwithstanding the efforts made at home.  The studies also indicate that stage
three can last forever.  The “preference” stage is the most significant stage
because it has a “value judgement” attached.  This is the time, in some

significant impact on the issue of cultural or religious identity.  For

]

When I read the trial record prepared by the parties, it seemed, as
Mr. Schwartz submits, that Lisa started with a plan to move closer to Gary
Finklestein and that all of her actions at trial should be seen with that
background in mind.  In other words, Mr. Schwartz argues that Lisa had her own
interests in mind and not those of the children’s.  It was against this
background that I listened to and examined the evidence heard at this very
lengthy trial.

[
224
]

Having heard the evidence I can say that, although her move to the
Thornhill area was made emotionally easier because she was moving closer to
Gary, Lisa in no way tried to sacrifice the interests of Abby and Ben in this
process.  Having listened to all of the principal participants in this trial, I
find that Lisa focused on a long-term future for the children.  She did so in a
manner that would be in keeping with her agreement with Bill to raise the
children with a strong Jewish identity.

[
225
]

Much was made of the fact that Lisa chose Uxbridge/Sunderland and,
therefore, because of that initial choice, some scepticism should be applied
when examining her motives.

[
226
]

In the first place, I accept Lisa’s evidence that her living in
Uxbridge/Sunderland was not going to be forever.  Secondly, even if Lisa felt
she should remain and allow the children to remain in Uxbridge/Sunderland for
the foreseeable future, that would have meant sacrificing their Jewish identity
for reasons already explained.

[
227
]

It might be very easy to find fault with Lisa by blaming her for the
separation and to focus on how matters were handled in her marriage.  Blame and
fault finding, in my view, misses the point in this case.  It does not focus on
the children or their needs.  In focusing on their needs, I am not asked to
judge whether or not they should be brought up as Jews.  This is something that
their parents decided on a long time ago and they tried their best to follow a
plan to accomplish the goal.  Having decided that this path was in their
children’s best interests, it would be wrong for this court to lose focus and
concentrate on blameworthy adult conduct.  This is especially so, when it
appears that there is so much to gain and so little to lose for Abby and Ben by
making the decision I have made.

Gladys —  The Airport Incident

[
228
]

When the trial began, both parties were embroiled in full-scale
custody litigation in the sense that Lisa was seeking sole custody of the
children.  While joint custody had worked well until Lisa announced the move to
Thornhill, friction became apparent after that time.  Bill, feeling very
threatened by Lisa’s wish to relocate the children, became more demanding about
the location of the children’s extra curricular activities.  He wanted all of
them to take place in Uxbridge for obvious reasons, while Lisa wanted some of
the activities to take place in Thornhill.  The jockeying for tactical advantage
led to more aggravation and conflict.  Unfortunately, most custody litigation
seems to promote this type of behaviour.

[
229
]

As part of the custody case, Lisa focused on an incident involving
Gladys’ care of the children that caused her concern.  Bill and Catherine had
extended a vacation and needed Gladys’ help in returning the children to Lisa.
As a result of a mix-up at the airport, Gladys was late in returning the
children.  Lisa was frantic with worry.  When the children were finally
returned, Lisa although relieved, became quite angry with Gladys.  This was
most unfortunate for both, as their relationship had always been good and was a
very respectful one.  Gladys looked upon Lisa as a daughter.  Gladys’ care for
the children was most appreciated by Lisa.

[
230
]

The airport incident was played up as demonstrating that Gladys was
getting older and, therefore, somewhat confused.  The point was to demonstrate
that her care for her grandchildren was not as good as it should be or once
was.  Along this line, Gladys was also portrayed as a person without computer
skills and, somehow, therefore, not being able to offer the best to Abby and
Ben.

[
231
]

I want to be absolutely clear about Gladys.  Lisa, Bill, and the
children are most fortunate to have her in their lives.  She is an excellent
example of a grandmother who knows how to care for children.  She has given her
grandchildren her best and her best has been excellent.  The children could not
ask for a better grandparent.  She is devoted to Abby and Ben, as they are to
her.

[
232
]

The airport incident came about because Gladys could not clearly
hear the directions she was given for the airport pickup.  This could have
happened to anyone.  She then had to feed the children because they were
hungry.  She was unable to contact Lisa.  Of course, Lisa was concerned;
however, once again, as with many other incidents in this case, it was blown
out of proportion because of the need to win a custody fight.

Other Evidence

[
233
]

In addition to the witnesses whose evidence has already been commented
upon, I also heard testimony from Lisa’s uncle, Alan Schwartz and from a former
neighbour of Lisa and Bill’s, namely, Sharon Runnals.  Much of their evidence
related to the issue of custody as opposed to the issue of schooling.
Nonetheless, both witnesses were helpful in giving me further insight as to the
character of each of Lisa and Bill and their parenting abilities.  Had the
parties been unable to resolve the custody issue, their evidence would have
been more germane to the issues I would have had to decide.

[
234
]

Evidence I heard with respect to the issues of school registration,
medical practitioners, local hospital services, and Lisa’s work location also
played a very minor role in assisting me with the decision.
